paragraphs.heading: Finding the best choice
paragraphs.text: Linear programming, also called linear optimization, is a way to find the best possible outcome, such as the highest profit or the lowest cost, in a model built from linear relationships. It is a special case of mathematical optimization. Put more precisely, you make a linear objective function as large or as small as possible while obeying constraints that are linear equations or linear inequalities.

paragraphs.heading: The shape of the problem
paragraphs.text: Together the constraints mark out the feasible region, the set over which the objective is optimized. That region is a convex polytope: the overlap of finitely many half spaces, each one set by a single linear inequality. The objective function is defined on this polytope. A linear programming algorithm looks for a point in it where the function is largest or smallest, if such a point exists.

paragraphs.heading: Where it is used
paragraphs.text: Linear programming is used heavily in mathematics and, less so, in business, economics and some engineering. Transportation, energy, telecommunications and manufacturing all use its models. It has helped describe problems of planning, routing, scheduling, assignment and design.

paragraphs.heading: From Fourier to the war
paragraphs.text: Solving a system of linear inequalities is an old problem: Fourier published a method for it in 1827. In the late 1930s the Soviet mathematician Leonid Kantorovich and the American economist Wassily Leontief each looked at practical uses on their own, Kantorovich for manufacturing schedules and Leontief for economics. Their work was largely ignored for decades. The turning point was World War II, when linear programming was used for transportation logistics, scheduling and resource allocation.

paragraphs.heading: Dantzig and the simplex method
paragraphs.text: Dantzig developed a general form of linear programming for planning problems in the US Air Force. In 1947 he invented the simplex method, which for the first time solved the problem efficiently in most cases. When he met John von Neumann to talk it over, von Neumann at once conjectured the theory of duality, seeing that a game theory problem he had been working on was equivalent. In 1975 Kantorovich and Koopmans split the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences; Koopmans had also framed classical economic problems as linear programs.

paragraphs.heading: Seventy people, seventy jobs
paragraphs.text: Dantzig's original example was finding the best way to assign 70 people to 70 jobs. Testing every possible arrangement would take vast computing power, since the number of arrangements is larger than the number of particles in the observable universe. Posed as a linear program and fed to the simplex algorithm, the best answer takes only a moment to find. The theory hugely cuts down how many possible solutions have to be checked.

paragraphs.heading: Later breakthroughs
paragraphs.text: In 1979 Leonid Khachiyan first showed that the problem can be solved in polynomial time. Then in 1984 Narendra Karmarkar brought in a new interior-point method, a larger breakthrough both in theory and in practice.
